subject: Critical Thinking
subcategory: Evidence & Truth: How We Know What's Real
title: Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance
description: A quick win: understand Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance.

hook.text: A study finds that a drug reduces blood pressure by 0.5 mmHg. Statistically significant. Clinically meaningless.

buildup.text: Statistical significance means the result is unlikely due to chance. It says nothing about the size of the effect.

discovery.text: Practical significance asks: is the effect large enough to matter in the real world?

twist.text: With 10 million participants, even trivial differences become 'significant.' The p-value is a function of sample size.

climax.text: Always ask two questions: 'Is it statistically significant?' AND 'Is the effect large enough to matter?'

punchline.text: Significant doesn't mean important. Read the effect size.

quiz.question: What does statistical significance (p < 0.05) actually tell us?
options: The result is unlikely due to chance alone
The effect is large enough to matter

details.summary: Statistical significance means a result is unlikely due to chance alone. Practical significance means the result is large enough to matter in the real world. A statistically significant weight loss of 0.2 pounds is meaningless in practice.
details.whyItMatters: Confusing statistical and practical significance leads to misinterpreting studies and making decisions based on real but trivially small effects.
takeaways: Statistical significance says the effect is probably real
Practical significance says the effect is large enough to matter
Large sample sizes can make trivial effects statistically significant

faq.question: Why can a statistically significant finding be practically meaningless?
faq.answer: With a large enough sample, even a tiny effect becomes statistically significant. A drug that lowers blood pressure by 0.1 mmHg might achieve p < 0.05 with millions of participants, but the effect is too small to matter clinically.

faq.question: How should you evaluate whether a study's findings are practically significant?
faq.answer: Look at the effect size, not just the p-value. Ask whether the magnitude of the effect would change behavior or outcomes in the real world. If the effect is real but tiny, it may be statistically significant but practically irrelevant.
